tagline.text: A Renaissance-style Augustinian church that has watched over the town at the foot of Mount Arayat

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (around the November 25 parish feast is a good time)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (a full day if combined with Mount Arayat)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,000 (including transport from Manila, per person for a day trip)

children.text: This is the Santa Catalina de Alexandria church in the middle of Arayat, Pampanga. The parish grew out of an Augustinian mission in 1590, and the three-level Renaissance facade and the long, roughly 70 m building stand out. It pairs well with a Mount Arayat trek.

The formal name of the church is the Parish Church of Santa Catalina de Alexandria, known in English as Saint Catherine of Alexandria Parish Church and simply as Arayat Church by locals. It stands in the town proper (Poblacion) of Arayat, Pampanga, and is an active parish within the Archdiocese of San Fernando, belonging to the
Vicariate of Mary, Help of Christians
. It is not a building preserved only for tourists. Mass is still held here every day, so you can see local people coming and going, which is much of its charm.

Its history goes back to the Spanish colonial period. On August 29, 1590, Bishop Domingo Salazar approved the Augustinians' request to found their first mission in Arayat, and Fray Juan de Valderrama began the work. Around 1600 the parish was established under Fray Contreras and placed under the patronage of Saint Catherine (Catalina) of Alexandria, a virgin martyr of the 4th century. The present stone and brick building is said to date from 1753, and church records show baptisms performed by Fray Villalobos from 1758. Sources differ on when it was built, so treat the exact year as a rough guide. The town itself is also old. According to tradition, people were already living here in the 14th century, and by around 1571 it was an important river trading town. Several stories about its origin exist, including that it was founded by the Majapahit-line noble Balagtas or his son Araw, but nothing is certain. Knowing this background, you can begin to imagine why Spanish missionaries set up a mission so early in this riverside town. The Poblacion where the church stands has the town hall, market and eateries close together and is easy to explore on foot.

The building was heavily reworked in the 19th century. Fray Jose Torres began rebuilding it in 1858, and his successor Fray Juan Tarrero could not finish because the Philippine Revolution broke out. Fray Urbano Bedoya finally completed the restoration in 1892, and decoration and repairs continued during the first two decades of the 20th century. A marble plaque above the entrance is said to name Juan Medina and Luisa Gabriel, donors of 20,000 pesos for repairs in 1923, in Spanish. It measures about 70 m long, 16 m wide and 12 m high, which is quite large for a country town church.

For visitors the church matters in three ways. First, it is a Spanish-era church in a town landscape backed by Mount Arayat, which rises alone from the Pampanga plain. Second, it lets you see Kapampangan faith and festival culture up close. Every year on the parish feast on November 25, a procession carries the image of Saint Catherine through town. Third, it can be one stop on a Pampanga church tour (Visita Iglesia) together with the churches of San Fernando and Bacolor. It is not a glamorous tourist attraction, so you will enjoy it most if you walk around quietly and appreciate the architecture.

The three-level Renaissance facade is the church's greatest sight. The second level has a frontal arcade, and the sides show cross-shaped windows reminiscent of Celtic crosses. The pediment has a blind pointed arch and a small semicircular window, so you can enjoy it twice: once from afar for the whole, and once up close for the details.

blocks.title: The saint at the portico and the main altar

children.text: An image of the patron saint, Santa Catalina, stands at the entrance portico, and an old image is said to be enshrined at the main altar. Saint Catherine is often shown with a wheel and a sword, so it is fun to look for such symbols when you see the images.

Above the main door is a Spanish marble plaque said to honor the donors of 20,000 pesos for repairs in 1923. It is a small record of how townspeople looked after their church a century ago, so look up and do not walk past it.

The left bell tower is said to have originally had chamfered corners and a domed roof, but now has intersecting gable roofs. The walls have been repainted and repaired many times and keep the feel of an old building, giving a different atmosphere from a perfectly restored church.

blocks.title: A long nave of about 70 m

children.text: With a length of about 70 m and a width of about 16 m, the nave is large even compared with other town churches in Pampanga. When it is not Mass time, step in quietly and look toward the altar at the end of the long central aisle to appreciate its scale.

Arayat holds its parish fiesta every year on November 25, the feast of Saint Catherine. A procession carrying the saint's image through town and various activities are said to take place, so if your timing fits it is a good way to feel local life. Events and schedules differ each year, so check the latest announcements.

blocks.title: A town with Mount Arayat in view

children.text: Arayat is an old riverside trading town at the foot of Mount Arayat, which rises alone from the Pampanga plain. As you walk around the church there are moments when the mountain comes into view, so you can aim for a photo that captures the church and the mountain in one scene.
Arriving for the morning Mass (in Kapampangan) lets you see everyday life among local worshippers. If you only want to look around, stay quietly at the back during Mass. Mass times may change.
After Mass, walk once around the outside of the church and look at the multi-level facade, the cross-shaped windows and the bell tower.
See the plaque above the main door and the saint at the portico, then, where permitted, go inside to see the long central aisle and the main altar.
Have breakfast at the market or an eatery near the church and enjoy the town atmosphere.
The church itself takes about an hour, so it is best combined with other plans.
Leave Manila early in the morning and arrive in Arayat.
Look around the church.
Head toward Mount Arayat National Park by tricycle or vehicle. Trekking is usually done with a guide, so confirm locally.
Come down and move on to San Fernando or Angeles for a late lunch or early dinner.
Arayat is about
from Manila (about 66km in a straight line; road distance varies by source at 70–90km). Depending on traffic it can take
2–3 hours
or more.
Provincial buses to Arayat have run from the Araneta Center (Cubao) bus terminal. According to a 2026 blog, buses from Cubao to San Fernando, Dau or Angeles cost about
, and a fare of about ₱180 to Arayat was reported a few years ago. Routes and fares change, so check locally.
If there is no direct bus, you can take a bus to Dau (Mabalacat), Angeles or San Fernando and transfer to a jeepney or tricycle.
Highways north of Manila get congested on weekends and holidays, so leave early.

items.title: By car or taxi from Manila

children.text: From Manila, take the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) and roads toward San Fernando into Arayat. Arayat is about
22km
from San Fernando and about
7km
from Santa Ana.
With a rented vehicle you can combine Mount Arayat and other Pampanga churches in one day.
The nearest international airport is Clark International Airport (CRK). From the airport, head toward Angeles or Dau and continue overland.
If you arrive at Manila's airport (NAIA), the usual way is to go up to Pampanga by bus or car.
The church is in the Poblacion and easy to reach on foot from the town center.
For Mount Arayat or other towns, use tricycles and jeepneys. Fares vary with distance and bargaining, so confirm before you ride.
The church is easiest to visit in the dry season with less rain. Morning or late afternoon is cooler and gives better photos of the facade.

Visiting around the November 25 parish feast lets you see festival atmosphere such as the procession, but crowds gather and roads can be congested. If you want to see the architecture quietly, a weekday morning is better.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Comfortable for both sightseeing and mountain trekking. Around the November 25 feast it can be crowded.
Midday is very hot. Look around early in the morning and bring water and a hat.
Showers are frequent and travel is difficult during typhoons. Check the weather forecast.

Arayat town does not have many tourist hotels, so most people visit as a day trip. To stay overnight, you will have more choices by booking in nearby San Fernando or Angeles and Clark and traveling in. A resort is reported near Mount Arayat, but check locally whether it is operating.

For meals, try Kapampangan food at the market and local eateries near the church. Pampanga is called the culinary capital of the Philippines, and dishes such as sisig are famous. If you go out to Angeles or San Fernando there are more varied restaurants.
Keep quiet during Mass and avoid flash photography. Mass times (weekdays 6 a.m.; Sundays 6 a.m., 8 a.m. and 5 p.m.) may change, so check the parish announcements.
Modest clothing that covers shoulders and knees is best.
Opening hours inside the church may not be fixed, so going around Mass times makes it easier to get inside.
If you combine it with a Mount Arayat trek, see the church first in the morning and climb the mountain in the morning. Showers are frequent in the afternoon.
If you continue to the churches of San Fernando and Bacolor, it becomes a Pampanga church tour.
Bring small cash (pesos). Cards are not accepted at many tricycles and markets.
Bring water, a hat and sunscreen. There may be little shade outside the church.
Check local conditions in parish announcements, such as the Arayat parish Facebook page.
Because it is an active parish church, avoid sightseeing photography and entry during Mass, funerals, weddings and other events.
Opening hours inside the church and Mass times may change, so check the latest announcements before visiting.
Dates of construction and rebuilding differ among sources. Give priority to on-site signs and local explanations.
Highway sections north of Manila are heavily congested on weekends and holidays. Allow extra time.
In the rainy season, heavy rain and typhoons make travel difficult and some stretches may flood.
Watch for pickpockets and keep valuables close to your body.
The symbolic mountain of Pampanga, close to the church, has a national park and trekking trails. A guide is usually required, and entrance and guide fees should be confirmed locally.
The central city of Pampanga, about
22km
from Arayat. It has many churches and restaurants and is good for meals or lodging.
Another Pampanga church, famous for being half buried by volcanic mudflows. It combines well in a church tour.
A city close to Clark International Airport, a good base when going from the airport to Arayat.
